statements.quote: Type the words **"The capital of France is "** into a chat model.
The next token comes back: **"Paris"**.
Most users treat this as ordinary.
It is, arguably, the deepest open question in modern AI, dressed up as a trivia question.
The picture we sketch in this chapter is the best current answer that the mechanistic interpretability community has been able to put together.
Each piece is backed by experiments on real models.
Each piece is also incomplete.
We will be honest about both.
*Nobody* knows the full story, not the model authors, not the interpretability researchers, not the theorists.
What we have is a stack of partial theories, each with published evidence, that together form a coherent working picture.
The picture is, by the consensus of the field, *almost certainly not the whole picture*.
It is doing a lot of work in the question "how does it know to reply Paris?", and most of that work is misleading.
- declarative memory in the human sense,
- a symbolic reasoning step,
- the model "understanding" geography.
We mean something much more specific and much more boring.
The trained model is a function
The whole rest of this chapter is an answer to that question, in eleven pieces, with the bits we don't know labelled honestly as we go.
A language model is trained to do one thing: predict the next token in a sequence.
It is *not* trained on a curriculum of trivia questions, and it is *not* given a goal of being factually accurate.
It is trained on a slice of human text, with the loss $-\log P(t_{i+1} \mid t_1, \ldots, t_i)$.
The fact "the capital of France is Paris" is only useful to the model insofar as it lowers that loss on internet text.

If, in some hypothetical corpus, every sentence that started "the capital of France is" were followed by the word "Lyon", the model would learn "Lyon" with equal enthusiasm, and with the same kind of internal mechanism.
This is what people mean when they say language models have no "ground truth" — they are not in the business of truth, they are in the business of likelihood.
That a likelihood-maximizer ends up saying anything we would call a fact at all is itself one of the surprises of the last decade, and it is what makes the question worth asking.
The forward pass that turns "The capital of France is " into a distribution over next tokens is short.

statements.quote: The residual stream is a *public* scratchpad: every attention head and every MLP layer reads from it and writes to it.
statements.section: The residual stream as a public scratchpad

statements.quote: The crucial word is *additive*: nothing in the architecture forces components to overwrite each other, they just add their contributions.
statements.section: The residual stream as a public scratchpad

statements.quote: This means a circuit for any specific behavior can be isolated as a sum of contributions from specific components at specific layers (\cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}).
statements.section: The residual stream as a public scratchpad

statements.quote: For the prompt "The capital of France is ", the first thing the model has to do is *figure out which tokens matter*.
The word "is" is a verb that wants an object.
The country is "France", which appeared three tokens earlier.
The mechanism for this routing is **self-attention** (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}).
Each attention head computes three projections of the residual stream at every position:
The attention pattern is the softmax of query-key dot products:
For our prompt, in the early layers, attention is mostly doing *local* work — each token looks at its neighbours.
By the middle layers, particular attention heads have learned to route specific pieces of information.
One head, in some layer, becomes a "previous-token head" that attends to whatever came immediately before each token.
Another head, in a later layer, learns to attend *from the final position back to the position where "France" sits* (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}).
The result is that the residual stream at the final position ends up containing information about "France" that the embedding alone did not put there.
If attention is the routing layer — the part that figures out *which* information matters — then the **MLP layers** are where the *content* of the model's knowledge actually lives.
statements.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

statements.quote: This is the most important conceptual claim in this chapter, and it has substantial experimental support.
statements.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

statements.quote: A Transformer block's MLP is a two-layer feed-forward network applied independently at every position:
statements.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

statements.quote: A hard hash table stores a fact or it doesn't.
statements.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

statements.quote: A soft key-value memory does something more interesting: it stores *fuzzy* facts.
statements.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

statements.quote: The key "the capital of France is" and the key "France's capital is" can both partially activate the same value vector — that's why the model answers Paris whether you phrase the question as "the capital of France is", "what is the capital of France", or "Paris is the capital of".
statements.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

statements.quote: In a hard lookup world, only one of those phrasings would hit.
statements.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

statements.quote: The fuzziness is what makes the model robust to paraphrase.
statements.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

statements.quote: So there is a cloud of soft key-value pairs in the model's weights.
The question is: is "Paris is the capital of France" stored *somewhere specific*, or is it smeared across millions of pairs in some inseparable way?
The experimental evidence from the last few years is, surprisingly clearly: *somewhere specific*.
\cite[Dai et al. (2022)]{dai2022knowledgeneurons} introduced the **knowledge neuron** framework.
For a relational fact like "the Space Needle is in Seattle", they:
Run the cloze query "The Space Needle is located in the city of \_\_\_" through the model and identify the layer where the answer first becomes confidently "Seattle".
Use integrated-gradients attribution to find which neurons in that layer's MLP, and which intermediate dimensions in the residual stream, are most responsible for the prediction.
**Suppress** those neurons (set their activations to zero) and watch the prediction collapse to "Seattle" → other plausible city, or "Seattle" → something unrelated.
**Amplify** those neurons and watch the prediction become over-confidently "Seattle" even in contexts where it shouldn't.
For BERT-style models, they find a small number of mid-layer MLP neurons whose activation is robustly correlated with the expression of specific facts.

The correlations are not perfectly monosemantic (more on this in §9), but they are strong enough to suggest that the model *is* doing something like "for this subject–relation pair, write the corresponding object into the residual stream" at identifiable locations.
This is the closest thing we have to a smoking gun: there exist *local, causally important* sites in the network for specific factual associations.
Not a single "grandmother cell" — a small cluster of mid-layer MLP neurons acting as a soft key-value pair.

The most dramatic experimental evidence that facts live in identifiable, narrow regions of the weights comes from (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022locating}) and their method **ROME** — *Rank-One Model Editing*.
Identify, for a specific factual prompt like "The Eiffel Tower is in", *which* mid-layer MLP block in the model (they studied GPT-J) is most responsible for the prediction "Paris".
They do this with causal tracing: they run the model, then re-run it with one component at a time replaced by a corrupted version, and measure how much the prediction degrades.
Confirm that the responsible block is small in scope: most other facts are unaffected by perturbations to that block.

The result: after the edit, the model says Rome when asked about the Eiffel Tower, says Rome when asked "Where is the Eiffel Tower?", says Rome when given "Eiffel Tower: ___" — and, crucially, *still says Paris when asked about the capital of France*.
The new fact is added without disrupting nearby facts.
This is more than an editing trick.
It is direct experimental evidence that **factual associations are stored as low-rank, locally-modifiable structures in the weights**.
If facts were smeared diffusely across the network, no rank-one update could change one without ruining others.

The fact that this works — and works robustly across many subjects and relations (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022memit}) — is the strongest evidence we have that the soft-key-value-memory picture in §4 is more than just an analogy.

The same low-rank, locally-editable structure shows up on the attention side: a head's influence on a head several layers later is carried by the dominant singular direction of its value–output matrix, and zeroing that one singular value measurably changes what the model does (\cite[Merullo et al., 2024]{merullo2024talkingheads}) (see [Mechanistic Interpretability](mechanistic_interpretability)).
ROME is not a complete theory of fact storage.
It is one experimental tool that shows *some* facts can be edited locally; it does not show that *all* facts are stored this way.
Multi-hop facts, rare facts, and facts that contradict earlier-trained facts are harder to edit cleanly.
And the edits sometimes do ripple, in ways that are not yet fully understood.
The picture in §4 is therefore a *best current model* of fact storage, with explicit annotations about where it is shaky.
The third piece of the picture is the most surprising, and the most contested.
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: A long line of work, going back to the famous "king − man + woman ≈ queen" result on word embeddings, has found that *semantic relations are linear operations in the model's representation space*.
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: (\cite[Park et al., 2024]{park2024linear}) made this rigorous with the **linear representation hypothesis**: a concept like "country → capital" is a *direction* in the residual stream, and the model's internal representations of words are arranged so that moving along that direction in the embedding of "France" lands you near the embedding of "Paris".
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: A related and equally striking line of evidence is the **function vector** finding of (\cite[Todd et al., 2024]{todd2024functionvectors}).
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: They give the model an in-context task — a few examples of "French: chien → dog; Spanish: gato → cat; English: ___ → ?" — and show that a small number of attention heads in the middle layers carry a *single vector* that encodes "the task is translate from {French, Spanish, English} to English".
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: They then extract that vector from one prompt, *inject* it into the residual stream of an entirely different prompt ("the cheese is ___"), and the model performs the translation task on the new prompt, even though the new prompt has no in-context examples.
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: This is the linear-representation + soft-key-value-memory picture in one breath.
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: It is the picture that *most* current interpretability researchers are betting on, and it has the strongest convergence between theory (Park et al.'s causal inner product) and experiment (ROME, function vectors, knowledge neurons).
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: The strongest evidence that this picture holds in *frontier-scale* production models — not just in the 100M–7B toys where most of the original experiments were done — comes from (\cite[Templeton et al., 2024]{templeton2024scaling}).
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: They trained sparse autoencoders on the residual stream of Claude 3 Sonnet and recovered up to 34 million interpretable features.
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: Among them: features for individual famous people, features for specific cities, features for specific code constructs, features for abstract concepts like "errors in code" and "sarcasm".
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: The fact that a feature for "the Eiffel Tower" exists as a *direction* in the residual stream of a production frontier model is direct confirmation that the linear-representation picture scales.
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: And the now-famous "Golden Gate Bridge" feature — a single direction whose activation makes the model insist on mentioning the bridge regardless of what you ask about — is a textbook example of a fact-as-direction.
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: This same "direction with a fixed meaning" scales from *facts* to whole *behaviors*.
statements.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

statements.quote: The country→capital relation above is one kind of axis; the [Mechanistic Interpretability](mechanistic_interpretability.php) lesson catalogs others — the truth, refusal, and honesty directions, sentiment and tone axes, and even where-and-when (spatial and temporal) directions — each found and verified the same way.

statements.quote: All of the above is the result of careful *post-hoc* analysis: you run the model, find what mattered, edit it, see what changes.
statements.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

statements.quote: There is also a much simpler trick that lets you *watch the answer form in real time* as the forward pass progresses: the **logit lens**.
statements.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

statements.quote: In a well-trained Transformer, the intermediate residual streams are already *approximately* in the unembedding basis (this is a consequence of the residual structure, weight decay, and the fact that the model is being trained end-to-end to produce a useful final residual stream).
statements.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

statements.quote: So the logits you get from intermediate layers are a meaningful, if imperfect, readout of "what would the model predict if it had to stop here?".
statements.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

statements.quote: There is a tempting picture that goes like this.
The residual stream starts somewhere — a vector near the embedding of " ", perturbed by attention that has read "France" from earlier.
As it passes through layer after layer, it gets *pulled* toward a region of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that decodes to "Paris".
Other prompts — "The capital of Germany is", "2 + 2 =", "Once upon a" — get pulled toward different regions.
The picture is of basins of attraction, like a Hopfield network or a dynamical system with fixed points.
This picture is *suggestive* and *partially grounded*, but it is not, as of this writing, a theorem.
Let us say what is and isn't known.
The connection between Transformer attention and modern Hopfield networks is mathematically precise.
(\cite[Ramsauer et al., 2020]{ramsauer2020hopfield}) showed that the attention update rule
with $\beta \propto 1/\sqrt{d_k}$, is *exactly* the update rule of a continuous-state Hopfield network with energy function
where $\mathrm{lse}$ is the log-sum-exp.
The classical Hopfield network of (\cite[Hopfield, 1982]{hopfield1982}) was the original "associative memory with basins of attraction" architecture.
So the *attention mechanism* in a Transformer is, formally, an iterative retrieval rule from a generalized Hopfield model.
That is a real mathematical fact.
From this, it is *tempting* to conclude that the whole residual stream is being "attracted" toward stored memory states across layers.
statements.section: What is suggested but not proven

statements.quote: The logit-lens evidence (§7) is consistent with this picture — predictions become more confident as layers progress, as if the residual stream is converging toward an attractor.
statements.section: What is suggested but not proven

statements.quote: The function-vector evidence (§6) is consistent — small vectors steer predictions, as if the residual stream were being gently pushed toward a different basin.
statements.section: What is suggested but not proven

statements.quote: Three honest problems with calling this "attractor dynamics" in the strict sense:
statements.section: What is wrong with the picture

statements.quote: **No energy function for the *whole* model.** Ramsauer et al.'s result gives an energy function for the *attention* operation alone.
statements.section: What is wrong with the picture

statements.quote: The MLP layers, the residual connections, and the layer-normalization steps between blocks do not obviously combine into a single energy function.
statements.section: What is wrong with the picture

statements.quote: Whether the full Transformer is a gradient-flow on some learned energy is an open conjecture, not a theorem.
statements.section: What is wrong with the picture

statements.quote: **Linear-ish, not nonlinear.** Real Hopfield dynamics are nonlinear, and "basin of attraction" is a nonlinear concept.
statements.section: What is wrong with the picture

statements.quote: The Transformer dynamics are mostly linear-ish (residual connections, layer norm) with isolated nonlinearities (softmax, GeLU).
statements.section: What is wrong with the picture

statements.quote: It is not clear that the language of basins carries over.
statements.section: What is wrong with the picture

statements.quote: So: the *attention* part of the Transformer is mathematically a Hopfield-style associative memory.
statements.section: What is wrong with the picture

statements.quote: The *whole* Transformer is, *maybe*, doing something attractor-like, but the evidence is empirical (logit lens, function vectors) and the formal justification is incomplete.
statements.section: What is wrong with the picture

statements.quote: You may have heard LLMs described as "high-dimensional dynamical systems", and dynamical systems make people think of chaos.
Let us be careful here, because the word *chaos* has a technical meaning (sensitivity to initial conditions, topological mixing, dense periodic orbits) that does not strictly apply.
The forward pass of an LLM is *deterministic*.
Given the same prompt and the same weights, you get the same logits.
So it is not literally chaotic in the sense of "small changes blow up exponentially over time".

What *is* true is that the learned function is **sensitive to its inputs in semantically meaningful ways**: a one-token change in the prompt ("The capital of France is" → "The capital of Germany is") produces a large, semantically coherent change in the output.
This is sensitivity *of the function*, not sensitivity *of a dynamical system*.
The word "chaos" is evocative but technically wrong here.
The forward pass is also, empirically, mostly **contractive**: semantically similar prompts land nearby in the residual stream.
That is the opposite of chaos.

So when this chapter says "the residual stream is being attracted toward a region that decodes to Paris", the right word is *attraction*, in the colloquial sense, not *chaos* in the dynamical-systems sense.
Take the analogy as a useful lens, not a literal claim about the math.
There is an obvious question lurking behind §4 and §5.
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: If facts live in MLP neurons, why is it that you cannot just open up a 7-billion-parameter model, look at the neurons one by one, and find the neuron that fires for "Paris"?
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: The answer is **superposition** (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}): the model represents more features than it has dimensions, by encoding features as nearly-orthogonal directions in activation space.
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: This is why the knowledge-neuron finding of (\cite[Dai et al., 2022]{dai2022knowledgeneurons}) is *remarkable*: it works *despite* superposition.
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: Some neurons end up monosemantic for specific facts because, during training, the optimization finds it cheaper to dedicate a few neurons to frequently-retrieved facts than to spread those facts across the superposition soup.
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: The systematic way to *recover* monosemantic features from a superposed residual stream is the **sparse autoencoder** (\cite[Cunningham et al., 2023]{cunningham2023sparse}; \cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{bricken2023monosemanticity}).
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: A sparse autoencoder is a small network trained to decompose the residual stream into a much larger dictionary of sparse features, such that each feature fires for a single human-interpretable concept.
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: The original SAE work \cite[Bricken et al. (2023)]{bricken2023monosemanticity} trained SAEs on the MLP of a one-layer transformer with 512 neurons, over 8 billion data points — not on GPT-2 small; \cite[Templeton et al. (2024)]{templeton2024scaling} then scaled the same idea to Claude 3 Sonnet and recovered up to 34 million features.
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: A parallel line of work \cite[Elhage et al. (2022)]{elhage2022solu} showed that an architectural change — replacing the GeLU activation in MLP neurons with a custom "SoLU" activation — makes individual neurons substantially *more* monosemantic even without SAEs, by reducing the incentive to use superposition in the first place.
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: This is an active research area; the current best SAEs recover tens of millions of interpretable features from a frontier model, and they have been used to find features that correlate with specific factual associations, specific syntactic structures, specific sentiment, and specific safety-relevant concepts.
statements.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

statements.quote: The picture in §3–§9 is the best current account, and it is the one most mechanistic interpretability researchers would defend at a conference.
It is also incomplete in ways that matter.
Almost all the experiments cited in this chapter — ROME, knowledge neurons, induction heads, logit lens — were done on models in the 100M–7B parameter range: BERT-base, GPT-2 small, GPT-J.
Frontier models in 2025–2026 are 100× to 1000× larger.
The honest version of this concern is that the picture in §3–§9 is well-supported for "small" production models (≤ 7B) and is rapidly being extended to frontier-scale production models.
(\cite[Templeton et al., 2024]{templeton2024scaling}) have trained sparse autoencoders on Claude 3 Sonnet and recovered millions of interpretable features.

(\cite[Lindsey et al., 2025]{lindsey2025biology}) and (\cite[Ameisen et al., 2025]{ameisen2025circuit}) have applied "circuit tracing" — replacing MLP layers with cross-layer transcoders and then following the computation feature-by-feature — to Claude 3.5 Haiku, producing the first end-to-end mechanistic accounts of multi-step behaviors in a production model.

The picture is converging: the same general mechanisms (residual stream as scratchpad, attention as routing, MLPs as soft key-value stores, facts as directions) appear to hold, with new layers of structure visible only at the frontier scale.
The picture works well for single-hop retrieval: "the capital of X is Y" → look up X, return Y.
It is much less clear for multi-hop: "the wife of the actor who played Batman in 1989 is".
This requires the model to *compose* several retrieved facts: identify Batman-1989 → Michael Keaton, identify Keaton's wife → Caroline McWilliams (or whoever the model thinks).
We do not have a clean mechanistic story for this.

There is some evidence that multi-hop reasoning uses chains of attention heads acting as a kind of scratchpad in the residual stream (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}), but it is not as crisp as the single-fact picture.
This is one of the most active areas of current research.
When the model says "Paris", is it because it has an internal *model* of the world in which France has a capital called Paris?
Or is it because it has memorized a soft key-value pair that happens to fire on this context?
The most striking evidence that LLMs *can* build internal models — not just lookups — comes from (\cite[Li et al., 2023]{li2022othello_iclr}).
They trained a GPT-style model on legal Othello moves *with no information about the board*.

Probing experiments revealed that the model had spontaneously built an internal representation of the board state, accurate enough that interventions on the representation produced the predicted changes in next-move predictions.
This is a *world model*, in a meaningful sense, learned purely from next-token prediction.
For factual knowledge about the real world, the situation is murkier.
Frontier models behave as if they have a *partial* world model: they can answer questions they were never directly trained on, by combining retrieved facts.

But it is unclear whether that world model is a coherent geometric structure in the residual stream (something like a map of Europe with Paris marked on it) or a vast, mostly-flat lookup table with cross-references.
Probably both, in unknown proportions.

The honest summary is that the *mechanism* of fact retrieval is reasonably well-understood at small scale and for single-hop facts, and that the *structure* of what is being retrieved — flat lookup vs. hierarchical world model — is one of the deepest open questions in interpretability.
A large part of what the model does is **binding**: tying a "filler" to a "gap" across distance — the subject to its verb, the object to the verb that governs it, a pronoun to its antecedent.
statements.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

statements.quote: The cleanest reverse-engineered case is the **indirect-object-identification circuit** (\cite[Wang et al., 2022]{wang2022interpretability}): a small set of heads whose job is to *copy* the right noun across the intervening verb to the position where it is needed.
statements.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

statements.quote: Understanding *why* this works sometimes and fails other times comes down to a single resource: **depth, as a budget of hops.**
statements.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

statements.quote: - **Nesting.** (\cite[Lakretz et al., 2021]{lakretz2020nested}) showed that long-distance agreement drops **below chance** on *nested* or embedded dependencies.
statements.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

statements.quote: When a second clause is wedged inside the first, the copy chain outgrows the effective depth and the errors compound — the model does not just get worse, it gets *systematically wrong*.
statements.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

statements.quote: - **Attractors.** (\cite[Lasri et al., 2022]{lasri2022agree}) showed that a **single** intervening "distractor" noun (an attractor with a mismatched number) is enough to hijack the copy and collapse subject-verb agreement.
statements.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

statements.quote: Here is the picture in one breath, with citations:

- **Attention** (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}; \cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}) routes information between positions: in our prompt, the critical job is making the final position attend back to the position holding "France".
- **Residual addition** (\cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}) accumulates these contributions into a single public vector.
- **Softmax** turns the logits into a probability distribution over the next token.
This picture has not come from any single experiment; it has been confirmed in pieces, each line of work tying a different mechanism to a specific, testable claim.

ROME (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022locating}) showed that a single rank-one edit to one mid-layer MLP block can rewrite one fact — the Eiffel Tower's city, say — while leaving its neighbours intact, and the successor method MEMIT (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022memit}) scaled the same locality result to thousands of simultaneous edits.
Knowledge-neuron attribution (\cite[Dai et al., 2022]{dai2022knowledgeneurons}) found that suppressing or amplifying a small cluster of MLP neurons flips a specific prediction on and off.
Function-vector steering (\cite[Todd et al., 2024]{todd2024functionvectors}) extracted the single residual-stream direction that encodes an in-context task and transplanted it into unrelated prompts.
Induction-head analysis (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}) identified the attention pattern that lets later tokens read earlier ones, which is what powers in-context learning.

The logit lens (\cite[nostalgebraist, 2020]{nostalgebraist2020logitlens}) and its refinement, the tuned lens (\cite[Belrose et al., 2023]{belrose2023tunedlens}), let you decode the residual stream at every layer and watch the answer form.

Superposition theory (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}) explains why none of these features lives in a single neuron — the model packs far more features than it has dimensions — and sparse autoencoders (\cite[Cunningham et al., 2023]{cunningham2023sparse}; \cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{bricken2023monosemanticity}) recover them as interpretable directions, scaled to a frontier production model by (\cite[Templeton et al., 2024]{templeton2024scaling}); the SoLU activation (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022solu}) attacks the same problem from the training side by reducing the incentive to superpose.

Anthropic's report "Mapping the mind of a large language model" (\cite[Anthropic, 2024]{anthropic2023mapping}) was the early accessible summary; the full machinery grew out of the Transformer Circuits Thread series, from the residual-stream framework (\cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}) and induction heads (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}) to superposition (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}), dictionary learning (\cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{bricken2023monosemanticity}), scaling monosemanticity (\cite[Templeton et al., 2024]{templeton2024scaling}), and circuit tracing in a production model (\cite[Ameisen et al., 2025]{ameisen2025circuit}; \cite[Lindsey et al., 2025]{lindsey2025biology}) — a series that has driven most of this story since 2021.

The picture is also consistent with the Hopfield-network interpretation of attention (\cite[Ramsauer et al., 2020]{ramsauer2020hopfield}), building on the classical associative-memory networks of \cite[Hopfield (1982)]{hopfield1982}.
It is not yet, however, the whole picture for frontier-scale models or multi-hop reasoning.
Those are open questions.
They are the questions the next decade of interpretability research will be asking.
Five things, restated as a checklist.
**Knowledge lives in the MLP layers as soft key-value pairs.** Attention is the routing layer; MLPs are the storage.
This is supported by ROME, knowledge neurons, and function vectors.
**Facts are directions in the residual stream.** "Capital of X" is a direction; adding it to the embedding of "France" gives you the embedding of "Paris".
This is the linear representation hypothesis, and it is the picture most consistent with all the experimental evidence.
**The picture is incomplete.** Scale gap, multi-hop composition, and the lookup-vs-world-model distinction are all open.
Anyone who tells you they have the full story is selling something.
If those five points are in your head, you understand roughly as much about fact retrieval in LLMs as any working researcher in 2026.
The remaining open questions are deep, but the parts we *do* know are now formally grounded, experimentally tested, and converging on a coherent picture.

blocks.quote: Type the words **"The capital of France is "** into a chat model. Press enter. The next token comes back: **"Paris"**. Most users treat this as ordinary. It is not. It is, arguably, the deepest open question in modern AI, dressed up as a trivia question.

The picture we sketch in this chapter is the best current answer that the mechanistic interpretability community has been able to put together. Each piece is backed by experiments on real models. Each piece is also incomplete. We will be honest about both. *Nobody* knows the full story, not the model authors, not the interpretability researchers, not the theorists. What we have is a stack of partial theories, each with published evidence, that together form a coherent working picture. The picture is, by the consensus of the field, *almost certainly not the whole picture*.
Where a fact lives
The question, re-framed
First, the word "knows". It is doing a lot of work in the question "how does it know to reply Paris?", and most of that work is misleading. We do **not** mean:
- conscious recall,
- declarative memory in the human sense,
- a database lookup,
- a symbolic reasoning step,
- the model "understanding" geography.
We mean something much more specific and much more boring. The trained model is a function
The whole rest of this chapter is an answer to that question, in eleven pieces, with the bits we don't know labelled honestly as we go.

A language model is trained to do one thing: predict the next token in a sequence. It is *not* trained on a curriculum of trivia questions, and it is *not* given a goal of being factually accurate. It is trained on a slice of human text, with the loss $-\log P(t_{i+1} \mid t_1, \ldots, t_i)$. The fact "the capital of France is Paris" is only useful to the model insofar as it lowers that loss on internet text. If, in some hypothetical corpus, every sentence that started "the capital of France is" were followed by the word "Lyon", the model would learn "Lyon" with equal enthusiasm, and with the same kind of internal mechanism. This is what people mean when they say language models have no "ground truth" — they are not in the business of truth, they are in the business of likelihood. That a likelihood-maximizer ends up saying anything we would call a fact at all is itself one of the surprises of the last decade, and it is what makes the question worth asking.
What the model actually computes, top to bottom
blocks.section: What the model actually computes, top to bottom

blocks.quote: The forward pass that turns "The capital of France is " into a distribution over next tokens is short. In a modern decoder-only Transformer like those behind GPT, Claude, and LLaMA, it looks like this:
blocks.section: What the model actually computes, top to bottom

blocks.quote: Five stages, each a deterministic matrix operation plus an elementwise nonlinearity.
blocks.section: What the model actually computes, top to bottom

blocks.quote: This sounds too austere to be true. The next sections will fill in how it can nevertheless produce Paris.
blocks.section: What the model actually computes, top to bottom

blocks.quote: The residual stream as a public scratchpad
blocks.section: The residual stream as a public scratchpad

blocks.quote: The residual stream is a *public* scratchpad: every attention head and every MLP layer reads from it and writes to it. The crucial word is *additive*: nothing in the architecture forces components to overwrite each other, they just add their contributions. This means a circuit for any specific behavior can be isolated as a sum of contributions from specific components at specific layers (\cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}).
blocks.section: The residual stream as a public scratchpad

blocks.quote: Attention: routing "France" to the end

For the prompt "The capital of France is ", the first thing the model has to do is *figure out which tokens matter*. The word "is" is a verb that wants an object. The object is a country. The country is "France", which appeared three tokens earlier. The mechanism for this routing is **self-attention** (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}).
Each attention head computes three projections of the residual stream at every position:
The attention pattern is the softmax of query-key dot products:

For our prompt, in the early layers, attention is mostly doing *local* work — each token looks at its neighbours. By the middle layers, particular attention heads have learned to route specific pieces of information. One head, in some layer, becomes a "previous-token head" that attends to whatever came immediately before each token. Another head, in a later layer, learns to attend *from the final position back to the position where "France" sits* (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}). The result is that the residual stream at the final position ends up containing information about "France" that the embedding alone did not put there.
The MLP as a soft key-value memory
blocks.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

blocks.quote: If attention is the routing layer — the part that figures out *which* information matters — then the **MLP layers** are where the *content* of the model's knowledge actually lives. This is the most important conceptual claim in this chapter, and it has substantial experimental support.
blocks.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

blocks.quote: A Transformer block's MLP is a two-layer feed-forward network applied independently at every position:
blocks.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

blocks.quote: A hard hash table stores a fact or it doesn't. A soft key-value memory does something more interesting: it stores *fuzzy* facts. The key "the capital of France is" and the key "France's capital is" can both partially activate the same value vector — that's why the model answers Paris whether you phrase the question as "the capital of France is", "what is the capital of France", or "Paris is the capital of". In a hard lookup world, only one of those phrasings would hit. The fuzziness is what makes the model robust to paraphrase.
blocks.section: The MLP as a soft key-value memory

blocks.quote: Where "Paris" specifically lives

So there is a cloud of soft key-value pairs in the model's weights. The question is: is "Paris is the capital of France" stored *somewhere specific*, or is it smeared across millions of pairs in some inseparable way? The experimental evidence from the last few years is, surprisingly clearly: *somewhere specific*.
\cite[Dai et al. (2022)]{dai2022knowledgeneurons} introduced the **knowledge neuron** framework. For a relational fact like "the Space Needle is in Seattle", they:
1. Run the cloze query "The Space Needle is located in the city of \_\_\_" through the model and identify the layer where the answer first becomes confidently "Seattle".
2. Use integrated-gradients attribution to find which neurons in that layer's MLP, and which intermediate dimensions in the residual stream, are most responsible for the prediction.
3. **Suppress** those neurons (set their activations to zero) and watch the prediction collapse to "Seattle" → other plausible city, or "Seattle" → something unrelated.
4. **Amplify** those neurons and watch the prediction become over-confidently "Seattle" even in contexts where it shouldn't.

For BERT-style models, they find a small number of mid-layer MLP neurons whose activation is robustly correlated with the expression of specific facts. The correlations are not perfectly monosemantic (more on this in §9), but they are strong enough to suggest that the model *is* doing something like "for this subject–relation pair, write the corresponding object into the residual stream" at identifiable locations.

This is the closest thing we have to a smoking gun: there exist *local, causally important* sites in the network for specific factual associations. Not a single "grandmother cell" — a small cluster of mid-layer MLP neurons acting as a soft key-value pair.
Editing and reading facts
Opening up one fact: ROME

The most dramatic experimental evidence that facts live in identifiable, narrow regions of the weights comes from (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022locating}) and their method **ROME** — *Rank-One Model Editing*.
Their procedure:

1. Identify, for a specific factual prompt like "The Eiffel Tower is in", *which* mid-layer MLP block in the model (they studied GPT-J) is most responsible for the prediction "Paris". They do this with causal tracing: they run the model, then re-run it with one component at a time replaced by a corrupted version, and measure how much the prediction degrades.
2. Confirm that the responsible block is small in scope: most other facts are unaffected by perturbations to that block.

The result: after the edit, the model says Rome when asked about the Eiffel Tower, says Rome when asked "Where is the Eiffel Tower?", says Rome when given "Eiffel Tower: ___" — and, crucially, *still says Paris when asked about the capital of France*. The edit is local. The new fact is added without disrupting nearby facts.

This is more than an editing trick. It is direct experimental evidence that **factual associations are stored as low-rank, locally-modifiable structures in the weights**. If facts were smeared diffusely across the network, no rank-one update could change one without ruining others. The fact that this works — and works robustly across many subjects and relations (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022memit}) — is the strongest evidence we have that the soft-key-value-memory picture in §4 is more than just an analogy. The same low-rank, locally-editable structure shows up on the attention side: a head's influence on a head several layers later is carried by the dominant singular direction of its value–output matrix, and zeroing that one singular value measurably changes what the model does (\cite[Merullo et al., 2024]{merullo2024talkingheads}) (see [Mechanistic Interpretability](mechanistic_interpretability)).

Honest caveats. ROME is not a complete theory of fact storage. It is one experimental tool that shows *some* facts can be edited locally; it does not show that *all* facts are stored this way. Multi-hop facts, rare facts, and facts that contradict earlier-trained facts are harder to edit cleanly. And the edits sometimes do ripple, in ways that are not yet fully understood. The picture in §4 is therefore a *best current model* of fact storage, with explicit annotations about where it is shaky.
Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis
blocks.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

blocks.quote: The third piece of the picture is the most surprising, and the most contested.
blocks.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

blocks.quote: A long line of work, going back to the famous "king − man + woman ≈ queen" result on word embeddings, has found that *semantic relations are linear operations in the model's representation space*. (\cite[Park et al., 2024]{park2024linear}) made this rigorous with the **linear representation hypothesis**: a concept like "country → capital" is a *direction* in the residual stream, and the model's internal representations of words are arranged so that moving along that direction in the embedding of "France" lands you near the embedding of "Paris".
blocks.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

blocks.quote: A related and equally striking line of evidence is the **function vector** finding of (\cite[Todd et al., 2024]{todd2024functionvectors}). They give the model an in-context task — a few examples of "French: chien → dog; Spanish: gato → cat; English: ___ → ?" — and show that a small number of attention heads in the middle layers carry a *single vector* that encodes "the task is translate from {French, Spanish, English} to English". They then extract that vector from one prompt, *inject* it into the residual stream of an entirely different prompt ("the cheese is ___"), and the model performs the translation task on the new prompt, even though the new prompt has no in-context examples.
blocks.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

blocks.quote: This is the linear-representation + soft-key-value-memory picture in one breath. It is the picture that *most* current interpretability researchers are betting on, and it has the strongest convergence between theory (Park et al.'s causal inner product) and experiment (ROME, function vectors, knowledge neurons).
blocks.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

blocks.quote: The strongest evidence that this picture holds in *frontier-scale* production models — not just in the 100M–7B toys where most of the original experiments were done — comes from (\cite[Templeton et al., 2024]{templeton2024scaling}). They trained sparse autoencoders on the residual stream of Claude 3 Sonnet and recovered up to 34 million interpretable features. Among them: features for individual famous people, features for specific cities, features for specific code constructs, features for abstract concepts like "errors in code" and "sarcasm". The fact that a feature for "the Eiffel Tower" exists as a *direction* in the residual stream of a production frontier model is direct confirmation that the linear-representation picture scales. And the now-famous "Golden Gate Bridge" feature — a single direction whose activation makes the model insist on mentioning the bridge regardless of what you ask about — is a textbook example of a fact-as-direction.
blocks.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

blocks.quote: This same "direction with a fixed meaning" scales from *facts* to whole *behaviors*. The country→capital relation above is one kind of axis; the [Mechanistic Interpretability](mechanistic_interpretability.php) lesson catalogs others — the truth, refusal, and honesty directions, sentiment and tone axes, and even where-and-when (spatial and temporal) directions — each found and verified the same way.
blocks.section: Facts as directions: the linear representation hypothesis

blocks.quote: Watching the answer form: the logit lens
blocks.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

blocks.quote: All of the above is the result of careful *post-hoc* analysis: you run the model, find what mattered, edit it, see what changes. There is also a much simpler trick that lets you *watch the answer form in real time* as the forward pass progresses: the **logit lens**.
blocks.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

blocks.quote: In a well-trained Transformer, the intermediate residual streams are already *approximately* in the unembedding basis (this is a consequence of the residual structure, weight decay, and the fact that the model is being trained end-to-end to produce a useful final residual stream). So the logits you get from intermediate layers are a meaningful, if imperfect, readout of "what would the model predict if it had to stop here?".
blocks.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

blocks.quote: Empirically, for a prompt like "The capital of France is", the logit-lens readout across layers looks something like:
blocks.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

blocks.quote: | Layer | Top decoded token | Interpretation |
blocks.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

blocks.quote: | 1–4 | "France", "Paris", "the" | shallow pattern matching; nothing confident yet |
blocks.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

blocks.quote: | 5–10 | "Paris", "Lyon", "Versailles" | the right semantic neighbourhood |
blocks.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

blocks.quote: | 15–25 | "Paris" with growing margin | the model has decided |
blocks.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

blocks.quote: | 30–40 | "Paris" with high margin | refinement, hedging, suppression of alternatives |
blocks.section: Watching the answer form: the logit lens

blocks.quote: What the picture gets right and wrong
blocks.section: What the picture gets right and wrong

blocks.quote: The attractor analogy, honestly

There is a tempting picture that goes like this. The residual stream starts somewhere — a vector near the embedding of " ", perturbed by attention that has read "France" from earlier. As it passes through layer after layer, it gets *pulled* toward a region of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that decodes to "Paris". Other prompts — "The capital of Germany is", "2 + 2 =", "Once upon a" — get pulled toward different regions. The picture is of basins of attraction, like a Hopfield network or a dynamical system with fixed points.
This picture is *suggestive* and *partially grounded*, but it is not, as of this writing, a theorem. Let us say what is and isn't known.
What is grounded
The connection between Transformer attention and modern Hopfield networks is mathematically precise. (\cite[Ramsauer et al., 2020]{ramsauer2020hopfield}) showed that the attention update rule
with $\beta \propto 1/\sqrt{d_k}$, is *exactly* the update rule of a continuous-state Hopfield network with energy function

where $\mathrm{lse}$ is the log-sum-exp. The classical Hopfield network of (\cite[Hopfield, 1982]{hopfield1982}) was the original "associative memory with basins of attraction" architecture. So the *attention mechanism* in a Transformer is, formally, an iterative retrieval rule from a generalized Hopfield model. That is a real mathematical fact.
What is suggested but not proven
blocks.section: What is suggested but not proven

blocks.quote: From this, it is *tempting* to conclude that the whole residual stream is being "attracted" toward stored memory states across layers. The logit-lens evidence (§7) is consistent with this picture — predictions become more confident as layers progress, as if the residual stream is converging toward an attractor. The function-vector evidence (§6) is consistent — small vectors steer predictions, as if the residual stream were being gently pushed toward a different basin.
blocks.section: What is suggested but not proven

blocks.quote: What is wrong with the picture
blocks.section: What is wrong with the picture

blocks.quote: Three honest problems with calling this "attractor dynamics" in the strict sense:
blocks.section: What is wrong with the picture

blocks.quote: 2. **No energy function for the *whole* model.** Ramsauer et al.'s result gives an energy function for the *attention* operation alone. The MLP layers, the residual connections, and the layer-normalization steps between blocks do not obviously combine into a single energy function. Whether the full Transformer is a gradient-flow on some learned energy is an open conjecture, not a theorem.
blocks.section: What is wrong with the picture

blocks.quote: 3. **Linear-ish, not nonlinear.** Real Hopfield dynamics are nonlinear, and "basin of attraction" is a nonlinear concept. The Transformer dynamics are mostly linear-ish (residual connections, layer norm) with isolated nonlinearities (softmax, GeLU). It is not clear that the language of basins carries over.
blocks.section: What is wrong with the picture

blocks.quote: So: the *attention* part of the Transformer is mathematically a Hopfield-style associative memory. The *whole* Transformer is, *maybe*, doing something attractor-like, but the evidence is empirical (logit lens, function vectors) and the formal justification is incomplete.
blocks.section: What is wrong with the picture

blocks.quote: On chaos theory

You may have heard LLMs described as "high-dimensional dynamical systems", and dynamical systems make people think of chaos. Let us be careful here, because the word *chaos* has a technical meaning (sensitivity to initial conditions, topological mixing, dense periodic orbits) that does not strictly apply.

The forward pass of an LLM is *deterministic*. Given the same prompt and the same weights, you get the same logits. So it is not literally chaotic in the sense of "small changes blow up exponentially over time". What *is* true is that the learned function is **sensitive to its inputs in semantically meaningful ways**: a one-token change in the prompt ("The capital of France is" → "The capital of Germany is") produces a large, semantically coherent change in the output. This is sensitivity *of the function*, not sensitivity *of a dynamical system*. The word "chaos" is evocative but technically wrong here.

The forward pass is also, empirically, mostly **contractive**: semantically similar prompts land nearby in the residual stream. That is the opposite of chaos. So when this chapter says "the residual stream is being attracted toward a region that decodes to Paris", the right word is *attraction*, in the colloquial sense, not *chaos* in the dynamical-systems sense. Take the analogy as a useful lens, not a literal claim about the math.
Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"
blocks.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

blocks.quote: There is an obvious question lurking behind §4 and §5. If facts live in MLP neurons, why is it that you cannot just open up a 7-billion-parameter model, look at the neurons one by one, and find the neuron that fires for "Paris"?
blocks.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

blocks.quote: The answer is **superposition** (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}): the model represents more features than it has dimensions, by encoding features as nearly-orthogonal directions in activation space.
blocks.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

blocks.quote: This is why the knowledge-neuron finding of (\cite[Dai et al., 2022]{dai2022knowledgeneurons}) is *remarkable*: it works *despite* superposition. Some neurons end up monosemantic for specific facts because, during training, the optimization finds it cheaper to dedicate a few neurons to frequently-retrieved facts than to spread those facts across the superposition soup.
blocks.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

blocks.quote: The systematic way to *recover* monosemantic features from a superposed residual stream is the **sparse autoencoder** (\cite[Cunningham et al., 2023]{cunningham2023sparse}; \cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{bricken2023monosemanticity}). A sparse autoencoder is a small network trained to decompose the residual stream into a much larger dictionary of sparse features, such that each feature fires for a single human-interpretable concept. The original SAE work \cite[Bricken et al. (2023)]{bricken2023monosemanticity} trained SAEs on the MLP of a one-layer transformer with 512 neurons, over 8 billion data points — not on GPT-2 small; \cite[Templeton et al. (2024)]{templeton2024scaling} then scaled the same idea to Claude 3 Sonnet and recovered up to 34 million features. A parallel line of work \cite[Elhage et al. (2022)]{elhage2022solu} showed that an architectural change — replacing the GeLU activation in MLP neurons with a custom "SoLU" activation — makes individual neurons substantially *more* monosemantic even without SAEs, by reducing the incentive to use superposition in the first place. This is an active research area; the current best SAEs recover tens of millions of interpretable features from a frontier model, and they have been used to find features that correlate with specific factual associations, specific syntactic structures, specific sentiment, and specific safety-relevant concepts.
blocks.section: Superposition: why there is no "grandmother cell"

blocks.quote: Three honest limits
The picture in §3–§9 is the best current account, and it is the one most mechanistic interpretability researchers would defend at a conference. It is also incomplete in ways that matter.
Scale gap

Almost all the experiments cited in this chapter — ROME, knowledge neurons, induction heads, logit lens — were done on models in the 100M–7B parameter range: BERT-base, GPT-2 small, GPT-J. Frontier models in 2025–2026 are 100× to 1000× larger. The honest version of this concern is that the picture in §3–§9 is well-supported for "small" production models (≤ 7B) and is rapidly being extended to frontier-scale production models. (\cite[Templeton et al., 2024]{templeton2024scaling}) have trained sparse autoencoders on Claude 3 Sonnet and recovered millions of interpretable features. (\cite[Lindsey et al., 2025]{lindsey2025biology}) and (\cite[Ameisen et al., 2025]{ameisen2025circuit}) have applied "circuit tracing" — replacing MLP layers with cross-layer transcoders and then following the computation feature-by-feature — to Claude 3.5 Haiku, producing the first end-to-end mechanistic accounts of multi-step behaviors in a production model. The picture is converging: the same general mechanisms (residual stream as scratchpad, attention as routing, MLPs as soft key-value stores, facts as directions) appear to hold, with new layers of structure visible only at the frontier scale.
Multi-hop and composition

The picture works well for single-hop retrieval: "the capital of X is Y" → look up X, return Y. It is much less clear for multi-hop: "the wife of the actor who played Batman in 1989 is". This requires the model to *compose* several retrieved facts: identify Batman-1989 → Michael Keaton, identify Keaton's wife → Caroline McWilliams (or whoever the model thinks). We do not have a clean mechanistic story for this. There is some evidence that multi-hop reasoning uses chains of attention heads acting as a kind of scratchpad in the residual stream (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}), but it is not as crisp as the single-fact picture. This is one of the most active areas of current research.
Facts vs. world models

When the model says "Paris", is it because it has an internal *model* of the world in which France has a capital called Paris? Or is it because it has memorized a soft key-value pair that happens to fire on this context?

The most striking evidence that LLMs *can* build internal models — not just lookups — comes from (\cite[Li et al., 2023]{li2022othello_iclr}). They trained a GPT-style model on legal Othello moves *with no information about the board*. Probing experiments revealed that the model had spontaneously built an internal representation of the board state, accurate enough that interventions on the representation produced the predicted changes in next-move predictions. This is a *world model*, in a meaningful sense, learned purely from next-token prediction.

For factual knowledge about the real world, the situation is murkier. Frontier models behave as if they have a *partial* world model: they can answer questions they were never directly trained on, by combining retrieved facts. But it is unclear whether that world model is a coherent geometric structure in the residual stream (something like a map of Europe with Paris marked on it) or a vast, mostly-flat lookup table with cross-references. Probably both, in unknown proportions.

The honest summary is that the *mechanism* of fact retrieval is reasonably well-understood at small scale and for single-hop facts, and that the *structure* of what is being retrieved — flat lookup vs. hierarchical world model — is one of the deepest open questions in interpretability.
Synthesis
Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks
blocks.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

blocks.quote: A large part of what the model does is **binding**: tying a "filler" to a "gap" across distance — the subject to its verb, the object to the verb that governs it, a pronoun to its antecedent. The cleanest reverse-engineered case is the **indirect-object-identification circuit** (\cite[Wang et al., 2022]{wang2022interpretability}): a small set of heads whose job is to *copy* the right noun across the intervening verb to the position where it is needed. Understanding *why* this works sometimes and fails other times comes down to a single resource: **depth, as a budget of hops.**
blocks.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

blocks.quote: - **Nesting.** (\cite[Lakretz et al., 2021]{lakretz2020nested}) showed that long-distance agreement drops **below chance** on *nested* or embedded dependencies. When a second clause is wedged inside the first, the copy chain outgrows the effective depth and the errors compound — the model does not just get worse, it gets *systematically wrong*.
blocks.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

blocks.quote: - **Attractors.** (\cite[Lasri et al., 2022]{lasri2022agree}) showed that a **single** intervening "distractor" noun (an attractor with a mismatched number) is enough to hijack the copy and collapse subject-verb agreement. The binding is a contest, and one rival token in the gap is often enough to win it.
blocks.section: Binding Across Distance — and Why It Breaks

blocks.quote: The takeaway is a clean one: **binding works for short, unambiguous chains, and it fails exactly when the chain is long, nested, or interfered with** — because every hop costs a layer, and the model is handed only a fixed number. This is the same depth-as-budget idea that caps the arithmetic of the algorithms chapter, and it is why "the model lost track of the subject" is not a quirk but a structural limit.

blocks.quote: Putting it together
Here is the picture in one breath, with citations:

- **Attention** (\cite[Vaswani et al., 2017]{vaswani2017attention}; \cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}) routes information between positions: in our prompt, the critical job is making the final position attend back to the position holding "France".
- **Residual addition** (\cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}) accumulates these contributions into a single public vector.
- **Softmax** turns the logits into a probability distribution over the next token.

This picture has not come from any single experiment; it has been confirmed in pieces, each line of work tying a different mechanism to a specific, testable claim. ROME (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022locating}) showed that a single rank-one edit to one mid-layer MLP block can rewrite one fact — the Eiffel Tower's city, say — while leaving its neighbours intact, and the successor method MEMIT (\cite[Meng et al., 2022]{meng2022memit}) scaled the same locality result to thousands of simultaneous edits. Knowledge-neuron attribution (\cite[Dai et al., 2022]{dai2022knowledgeneurons}) found that suppressing or amplifying a small cluster of MLP neurons flips a specific prediction on and off. Function-vector steering (\cite[Todd et al., 2024]{todd2024functionvectors}) extracted the single residual-stream direction that encodes an in-context task and transplanted it into unrelated prompts. Induction-head analysis (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}) identified the attention pattern that lets later tokens read earlier ones, which is what powers in-context learning. The logit lens (\cite[nostalgebraist, 2020]{nostalgebraist2020logitlens}) and its refinement, the tuned lens (\cite[Belrose et al., 2023]{belrose2023tunedlens}), let you decode the residual stream at every layer and watch the answer form. Superposition theory (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}) explains why none of these features lives in a single neuron — the model packs far more features than it has dimensions — and sparse autoencoders (\cite[Cunningham et al., 2023]{cunningham2023sparse}; \cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{bricken2023monosemanticity}) recover them as interpretable directions, scaled to a frontier production model by (\cite[Templeton et al., 2024]{templeton2024scaling}); the SoLU activation (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022solu}) attacks the same problem from the training side by reducing the incentive to superpose. Anthropic's report "Mapping the mind of a large language model" (\cite[Anthropic, 2024]{anthropic2023mapping}) was the early accessible summary; the full machinery grew out of the Transformer Circuits Thread series, from the residual-stream framework (\cite[Elhage et al., 2021]{elhage2021mathematical}) and induction heads (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}) to superposition (\cite[Elhage et al., 2022]{elhage2022superposition}), dictionary learning (\cite[Bricken et al., 2023]{bricken2023monosemanticity}), scaling monosemanticity (\cite[Templeton et al., 2024]{templeton2024scaling}), and circuit tracing in a production model (\cite[Ameisen et al., 2025]{ameisen2025circuit}; \cite[Lindsey et al., 2025]{lindsey2025biology}) — a series that has driven most of this story since 2021. The picture is also consistent with the Hopfield-network interpretation of attention (\cite[Ramsauer et al., 2020]{ramsauer2020hopfield}), building on the classical associative-memory networks of \cite[Hopfield (1982)]{hopfield1982}. It is not yet, however, the whole picture for frontier-scale models or multi-hop reasoning.
Those are open questions. They are the questions the next decade of interpretability research will be asking.
What to carry away
Five things, restated as a checklist.
2. **Knowledge lives in the MLP layers as soft key-value pairs.** Attention is the routing layer; MLPs are the storage. This is supported by ROME, knowledge neurons, and function vectors.

3. **Facts are directions in the residual stream.** "Capital of X" is a direction; adding it to the embedding of "France" gives you the embedding of "Paris". This is the linear representation hypothesis, and it is the picture most consistent with all the experimental evidence.
5. **The picture is incomplete.** Scale gap, multi-hop composition, and the lookup-vs-world-model distinction are all open. Anyone who tells you they have the full story is selling something.

If those five points are in your head, you understand roughly as much about fact retrieval in LLMs as any working researcher in 2026. The remaining open questions are deep, but the parts we *do* know are now formally grounded, experimentally tested, and converging on a coherent picture.
